</TD><A NAME="d10q_htm_tx59872_5"></A><TD valign=top width=598.4><P style="margin:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>MANAGEMENT&#146;S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS.</B></P>
</TD><TD valign=top width=1.333>&nbsp;</TD></TR>
</TABLE>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Executive Overview </B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Dow Jones &amp; Company is a leading provider of global business and financial news and information through newspapers, newswires, magazines, the Internet, indexes, licensing, television and radio. &nbsp;In addition, the Company owns general-interest community newspapers throughout the U.S. &nbsp;For the year ended December 31, 2005, approximately 50% of the Company&#146;s revenues were derived from the print publishing segment, which is primarily comprised of the global editions of <I>The Wall Street Journal</I>. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s overall financial results are largely dependent on the operating performance of <I>The Wall Street Journal</I>, which, to a significant extent, is dependent upon business-to-business (B2B) advertising placed in its publications, particularly from the financial and technology sectors. &nbsp;The electronic publishing segment, which includes newswires, online publishing, indexes and other electronic operations, comprised approximately 30% of the Company&#146;s revenue, while the remaining approximately 20% of total revenues were contributed from the general-interest community newspapers segment.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In 2005, while profits from our electronic publishing segment were particularly strong, our print publishing segment continued to face a difficult industry-wide print advertising environment. &nbsp;As a result, for the year, advertising linage at <I>The Wall Street Journal</I> declined 0.7%. &nbsp;Advertising in the Journal was down 7% in the first six months and up 6% in the latter six months aided by the September launch of the Weekend Edition and an increase in weekday advertising. &nbsp;While advertisers continue to decide their spending close to actual publication dates, making predictions difficult, we expect this improved trend to continue into the first quarter of 2006. &nbsp;We remain focused on improving quality, controlling our spending, sharpening our execution, improving under-performing businesses, and executing on the many strategic initiatives currently underway to reshape our portfolio and drive future growth. &nbsp;These initiatives include the acquisition of MarketWatch in January, the September launch of the Weekend Edition, the October 17 launch of new reformatted international compact editions of the Journal, and the recently announced content and design changes and planned web width reduction at the U.S. Journal to debut in January 2007. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>We expect that Weekend Edition will build off the success of our Weekend Journal and Personal Journal weekday sections in growing and diversifying our advertising customer base by attracting more consumer-oriented advertisers. &nbsp;We have a uniquely influential and affluent audience that not only makes large B2B spending decisions but also spends heavily on personal consumption items. &nbsp;The Weekend Edition enables advertisers to reach these readers in the right place at the right time &#150; at home on the weekend &#150; which is highly conducive to influencing their consumer spending decisions. &nbsp;More than 360 advertisers supported the Weekend Edition in 2005, with 55% of them new to the Journal. &nbsp;About 65% of the ad revenue is from consumer advertising, with only about 35% of it shifting from the weekday editions. &nbsp;While this initiative diluted earnings by about 11 cents per share in 2005, and is expected to dilute earnings in 2006 by about 15 cents per share, we believe that the Weekend Edition will be a major driver of long-term growth in revenue and earnings. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In October 2005, we announced a number of innovative design and content enhancements to the Journal's U.S. print edition, which will be made to better serve existing readers and attract new ones. &nbsp;These improvements will include changes to the Journal's organization, navigation and content--as well as stronger links to <I>WSJ.com</I>--designed to make accessing Journal content faster and more convenient for readers. &nbsp;Some of these enhancements will be introduced during 2006, culminating in January 2007 with a redesign of the Journal and reformatting to a more industry-standard 48-inch web width from its current 60-inch web width. &nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Retrofitting 19 presses in the Journal's 17 print sites to print the new web width is expected to be completed by January 2007 and the capital cost for such is estimated at $43 million, of which $3 million was expended in 2005, and we expect the remainder will be expended in 2006 ($36 million) and 2007 ($4 million). &nbsp;We will also incur about $13 million in one-time training, development and marketing costs for the project, $9 million of which will be incurred in 2006. &nbsp;The redesigned and newly formatted paper will launch in January 2007 and, excluding one-time start-up costs, we expect to save about $18 million per year in operating expenses (after about $4 million per year in non-cash depreciation expense), mainly from reduced newsprint consumption, starting in 2007. &nbsp;The project is expected to generate an after-tax return on investment of about 26% with a payback period of less than three years. &nbsp;This initiative is expected to dilute earnings in 2006 by about 7 cents per share and be accretive to earnings in 2007 and thereafter by about 13 cents per share. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>We have also undertaken a number of other initiatives to reshape our portfolio and to increase profits for the Company. &nbsp;In October 2005, we launched reformatted compact editions at our international editions in an easier to read format that is more tightly integrated with <I>WSJ.com</I> to better serve the needs of highly mobile international business leaders. &nbsp;We expect this international repositioning will not only improve annual profits by $17 million, mainly from reduced costs, but also drive increased revenue. &nbsp;During 2005 we also entered into an agreement to exit our unprofitable television partnerships with CNBC in Europe and Asia and in CNBC World, while maintaining our profitable licensing relationship with CNBC in the U.S. &nbsp;The exit is expected to eliminate about $15 million of annual pretax equity losses. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>16</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>On January 21, 2005, we completed the acquisition of MarketWatch for a purchase price of approximately $532 million, including certain transaction costs, significantly expanding our participation in online publishing. &nbsp;MarketWatch is a leading provider of company, markets and business news, financial information and analytical tools and operates two award-winning Web sites: MarketWatch.com and BigCharts.com. &nbsp;Prior to the acquisition these free, advertising-supported, sites served approximately seven million unique visitors per month with timely market news and information. &nbsp;MarketWatch also operates MarketWatch Licensing Services, which is a leading licensor of news, data, investment analysis tools and other online applications to financial services firms, media companies, and corporations for use mainly on their intranets and retail Web sites. &nbsp;MarketWatch has been fully integrated into our Consumer Electronic Publishing business, with extensive integration of its news, advertising sales, information technology and back office operations. &nbsp;The Company believes that the MarketWatch merger complements The Wall Street Journal Online Network, which provides premium business news to about three million unique visitors per month. &nbsp;By combining the traffic of The Wall Street Journal Online network and MarketWatch into the Dow Jones Online Network, our Web sites averaged approximately nine million unduplicated unique visitors per month during 2005. &nbsp;The combined Consumer Electronic Publishing business exceeded our profit expectations for 2005, largely due to higher than expected cost synergy savings on the MarketWatch integration.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>We are very proud to have won two additional Pulitzer prizes in 2005, one for health care coverage and the other for film criticism. &nbsp;These awards represent our 30<SUP>th</SUP> and 31<SUP>st</SUP> Pulitzers, and are especially gratifying as they were awarded in our new &#147;business of life&#148; coverage areas.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Finally, in the first quarter of 2006, we announced changes in our management and organizational structure. &nbsp;Effective February 1, 2006, Richard F. Zannino was named chief executive officer and elected to the board of directors. &nbsp;Peter R. Kann retired as chief executive officer as of such date and will continue as chairman until April 2007. &nbsp;Karen Elliott House, senior vice president of Dow Jones and publisher of <I>The Wall Street Journal</I>, also retired in February. &nbsp;Effective February 22, 2006, the Company established a new organizational structure pursuant to which it will organize and report its business around its three markets: &nbsp;consumer media, enterprise media, and community media. &nbsp;The Consumer Media Group is led by L. Gordon Crovitz, executive vice president of Dow Jones, president of Dow Jones Consumer Media Group, and publisher of The Wall Street Journal Franchise. &nbsp;The Enterprise Media Group is led by Clare Hart, executive vice president of Dow Jones and president of Dow Jones Enterprise Media Group. The Community Media Group is led by John Wilcox, senior vice president of Dow Jones, president of Dow Jones Community Media Group and chairman and chief executive officer of Ottaway Newspapers, Inc. &nbsp;The new structure is expected to result in cost savings of approximately $8 million per year, largely as a result of eliminating about 20 net positions. &nbsp;The Company expects to record a charge of approximately $11 million in the first quarter of 2006 reflecting employee severance and other costs.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>17</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Net Income </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Net income in 2005 was $60.4 million, or $.73 per diluted share, compared with net income in 2004 of $99.5 million, or $1.21 per share (all &#147;per share&#148; amounts included herein are based on reported net income and diluted weighted-average shares outstanding). &nbsp;Earnings per share in 2005 included certain items affecting comparisons that netted to a reduction in earnings of $.25 per share, while earnings in 2004 included certain items affecting comparisons that had no net effect on earnings per share. &nbsp;These items are detailed further beginning on page 29.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Revenues in 2005 increased $98.2 million, or 5.9%, to $1.77 billion, primarily reflecting the impact of recent acquisitions and strong organic growth at the Company&#146;s electronic publishing businesses partially offset by lower revenue at print publishing. &nbsp; Advertising revenue increased $15 million
, or 1.6%, as strong growth in online advertising, in part due to the MarketWatch acquisition,
 was partially offset by lower advertising revenue
at print publishing .
Information services revenues grew $83.1 million, or 25.3%, reflecting incremental revenue from MarketWatch as well as organic growth across electronic publishing. &nbsp;Circulation and other revenue was flat as higher revenue from <I>The Wall Street Journal</I>, was offset by lower circulation revenue at Ottaway and the Far Eastern Economic Review.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Expenses </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Operating expenses in 2005 increased $139.1 million, or 9.2%, to $1.65 billion, <A NAME="OLE_LINK18"></A>primarily reflecting incremental costs from MarketWatch (approximately five percentage points of the increase), incremental costs for Weekend Edition, higher newsprint costs and a restructuring charge recorded during the second quarter. &nbsp;Newsprint costs increased 9.9%, driven by an 11.8% increase in newsprint prices, partially offset by a 1.7% decline in consumption. &nbsp;The number of full-time employees at December 31, 2005, was 7,501 as compared to 7,143 last year. &nbsp;Excluding acquisitions, headcount was flat compared to last year.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U><BR></U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Income </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Operating income in 2005 was $121.3 million (6.9% of revenues), down $40.9 million, or 25.2%, from 2004 operating income of $162.2 million (9.7% of revenues), as higher profits at the Company&#146;s electronic publishing businesses were more than offset by a decline in profits at the Company&#146;s print publications, in part due to planned dilution related to the launch of the Weekend Edition, and restructuring charges.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Non-operating Loss</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Non-operating losses totaled $17.7 million compared to $4 million in 2004. &nbsp;The increase from 2004 was driven by the $35.9 million charge recorded to write-down the Company&#146;s investments in CNBC International and CNBC World and a $13.9 million increase in net interest expense as a result of borrowings to fund the MarketWatch acquisition. &nbsp;Partially offsetting these items were nearly $22.9 million of gains from investment dispositions and improved results from our equity investments. &nbsp;The investment write-downs and investment dispositions are detailed further beginning on page 29. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company&#146;s share of equity in earnings of associated companies in 2005 was $14.1 million compared with earnings of $2.4 million in 2004. &nbsp;The increase was driven by the elimination of international television losses, as well as improvement at Stoxx, <I>Vedomosti</I> and <I>SmartMoney</I>, which more than offset reduced equity earnings resulting from the sale of F.F. Soucy during the year. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><BR></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Net Income</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Net income in 2004 was $99.5 million, or $1.21 per diluted share, compared with 2003 earnings of $170.6 million, or $2.08 per share. &nbsp;Earnings per share in 2004 included certain items affecting comparisons that taken together had no net effect on earnings per share in 2004, while 2003 included certain items affecting comparisons that netted to a gain of $1.12 per share. &nbsp;These items are detailed further beginning on page 29. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U><BR></U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Revenues in 2004 increased $123 million, or 7.9%, to $1.7 billion. &nbsp;On a &#147;same property&#148; basis, meaning excluding properties divested or acquired during the preceding year, total revenue was up 4.9%. &nbsp;Advertising revenue was up 8.5% and, on a same property basis, increased 7.1%, primarily reflecting strong gains in advertising rates at the U.S. Journal and volume and rate gains at our community newspapers segment. &nbsp;Information services revenues were up 15% and, on a same property basis, increased 5.2%, reflecting strong organic growth at Consumer Electronic Publishing and Dow Jones Indexes/Ventures. &nbsp;Circulation and other revenue were up 1.7% and, on a same property basis, decreased slightly. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify> <BR>
</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Expenses</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Operating expenses in 2004 increased $103.7 million, or 7.4%, to $1.51 billion. &nbsp;Just over one percentage point of the increase was due to the fact that 2003 expenses were reduced by an $18.4 million gain on the settlement of a business interruption insurance claim, while the remaining increase reflected incremental costs from newly acquired properties (about three percentage points), and the balance was due to increases in employee compensation, newsprint usage and prices, and unfavorable changes in foreign currency exchange. &nbsp;Newsprint expense, on a same property basis, increased 8.5% as a result of a 6.5% increase in newsprint prices and a 1.9% increase in consumption. &nbsp;The number of full-time employees at December 31, 2004 was 7,143, up 2.4% from December 31, 2003, primarily reflecting additional employees from acquisitions.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify> <BR>
</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Income</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Operating income in 2004 was $162.2 million (9.7% of revenues), up $19.3 million, or 13.5%, from 2003 operating income of $142.9 million (9.2% of revenues). &nbsp;The increase in operating income reflected a 33% growth in operating income at our business segments, partially offset by the insurance gain in 2003, which did not recur in 2004.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B> <BR>
<BR>
</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>19</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Non-operating (Loss)/Income</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Non-operating losses totaled $4 million in 2004 compared with non-operating income of $79.4 million in 2003. &nbsp;Non-operating income in 2003 included a gain of $59.8 million related to the resolution of a loss contingency related to the sale of our former Telerate subsidiary, $6.7 million of interest income related to an IRS tax refund and a gain of $18.7 million from a non-monetary exchange of interests in <I>The</I> <I>Wall Street Journal Europe</I> and <I>Handelsblatt</I>, net of a $9.5 million charge related to the accretion of discount on a contract guarantee. &nbsp;Non-operating losses in 2004 included a $6.9 million charge related to the accretion of discount on the contract guarantee, net of a $3.3 million gain on the disposition of an investment. &nbsp;These items are detailed further beginning on page 29. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company&#146;s share of equity in earnings of associated companies in 2004 was $2.4 million compared with earnings of $2.9 million in 2003. &nbsp;The lower earnings primarily resulted from increased losses at CNBC International which was somewhat offset by improved results at Factiva, <I>SmartMoney</I> and <I>Vedomosti</I>. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Segment Data </B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company reports the results of its operations in three segments: print publishing, electronic publishing and community newspapers. &nbsp;In addition, the Company reports certain administrative activities under the corporate segment. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Print Publishing</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Print publishing, which is largely comprised of the global editions of <I>The Wall Street Journal</I>, publishes business and financial content world-wide. &nbsp;This content is published primarily in the U.S., Europe, Asia and Latin America editions of <I>The Wall Street Journal</I> and on U.S. television through a licensing agreement with CNBC. &nbsp;The Company manages the global Journal operations as one segment as their products comprise the global Journal brand, and there are significant interrelationships within the editions including global management, shared news flows and workforce and a global advertising customer base, sales force and pricing. &nbsp;U.S. television, which represents a licensing agreement with NBC Universal to provide branding, news content and on-air expertise to CNBC, is a further extension of the Journal brand and content. &nbsp;U.S. television contributes a significantly higher operating margin than the publications within the segment since it largely represents incremental revenue for the global Journal content and branding. &nbsp;The Company also includes the operations of <I>Barron&#146;s</I> within print publishing instead of reporting them separately because of their relative immateriality to the Company&#146;s results on a consolidated basis and because <I>Barron&#146;s</I> shares services with and its operations are similar to the global Journal. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In September 2005, the Company launched the Weekend Edition of <I>The Wall Street Journal</I>, which is expected to build off the success of the Weekend Journal and Personal Journal sections in attracting more consumer-oriented advertisers and reduce the reliance over time on B2B financial and technology advertising. &nbsp;The Weekend Edition is delivered to readers at home on Saturday mornings, enabling advertisers to reach readers in the right place at the right time, which is highly conducive to influencing their consumer spending decisions.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In October 2005, the Company launched reformatted compact international editions which are now in an easier to read format and are more tightly integrated with <I>WSJ.com</I> to better serve the needs of highly mobile international business leaders. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Print publishing revenues for 2005 decreased $32.7 million, or 3.4%, to $916.1 million, primarily driven by weakness in advertising revenue. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>U.S. Publications:<I> </I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>U.S. advertising revenue declined $26.8 million, or 4.4%, to $579.9 million, <A NAME="OLE_LINK29"></A>primarily from lower advertising yield and linage at <I>The Wall Street Journal </I>as well as lower television advertising revenue. &nbsp;At the U.S. Journal, general advertising linage, which represented 42.1% of total U.S. Journal linage, increased 1.2% on higher general B2B advertising, partially offset by declines in auto, travel and pharmaceutical advertising. &nbsp;Technology advertising, which represented 15.6% of total U.S. Journal linage, decreased 8.1%, on declines in all categories except personal computer and office products. &nbsp;Financial advertising, which represented 15.7% of total U.S. Journal linage, declined 14.9% as declines in wholesale, mutual funds and advisory advertising more than offset increases in tombstone and retail banking advertising. &nbsp;Classified and other advertising linage, the lowest yielding advertising category, increased 12.4% and represented 26.6% of total U.S. Journal linage. &nbsp;Color advertising pages increased 6%, and color premium revenue was up 19%. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>21</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Circulation and other revenue for the U.S. print publications increased $0.3 million to $260.6 million. &nbsp;Average circulation for <I>The Wall Street Journal</I> was 1,739,000 during 2005 compared with average circulation of 1,810,000 in 2004. &nbsp;The decline in average circulation was largely due to fewer bulk sale copies. &nbsp;Average circulation for <I>Barron&#146;s</I> was 298,000 in 2005 as compared to 299,000 in 2004.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>International Publications:</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>International print publication revenues declined $6.2 million, or 7.6%, to $75.6 million as increased advertising at <I>The Wall Street Journal Europe</I> and <I>The Wall Street Journal Asia</I> was more than offset by lower planned revenues from FEER, due to the repositioning from a weekly to a monthly publication that occurred during the fourth quarter of 2004. &nbsp;In October 2005, the Asian and European editions of the Journal were re-launched in new compact formats with enhanced linkages between print and online editions, which contributed to 12.3% and 29.3% linage increases in Asia and Europe, respectively, during the fourth quarter. &nbsp;International print circulation and other revenues declined $4.1 million, or 12.4%, also due to the repositioning of FEER. &nbsp;Combined average circulation for the international Journals was 169,000 in 2005 compared with 167,000 in 2004.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Expenses </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Print publishing expenses increased $21.9 million, or 2.4%, to $939.2 million, largely due to investments in Weekend Edition as well as higher marketing and newsprint expenses, which were partially offset by lower compensation costs on lower headcount. &nbsp;Newsprint costs increased 10.1%, reflecting an 11.7% increase in newsprint prices, partially offset by a 1.5% decline in consumption. &nbsp;The number of full-time employees in the print publishing segment decreased 2% as compared to last year. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Loss </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Print publishing&#146;s 2005 operating loss was $23.1 million compared to income of $31.5 million in 2004 (3.3% of revenues), reflecting planned dilution related to Weekend Edition as well as <A NAME="OLE_LINK28"></A>reduced profits at the U.S. Journal and U.S. television partially offset by reduced losses at the international editions.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><BR>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Print publishing revenues for 2004 increased $33.4 million, or 3.6%, to $948.8 million, reflecting advertising revenue gains at the U.S. publications. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>U.S. Publications:<I> </I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>U.S. print publication revenue increased $33.4 million, or 4%, to $867 million. &nbsp;U.S. print publication advertising revenue increased $36.3 million, or 6.4%, to $606.6 million, despite a 0.5% decrease in advertising linage at <I>The Wall Street Journal</I> as a result of higher ad yield (or revenue per page). &nbsp;General advertising, which represented about 41% of total U.S. Journal linage, increased 4% in 2004. &nbsp;The increase in general ad volume was driven by a 4% increase in consumer advertising linage and a 13% increase in consumer ad revenue, with gains in luxury and pharmaceuticals advertising, partially offset by a decline in auto advertising. &nbsp;Financial advertising, which accounted for 18% of total Journal linage, increased 7% with ad revenue up 15% in 2004. &nbsp;Financial ad volume improved as a result of strong gains in wholesale advertising coupled with increases in retail mutual funds advertising partially offset by weakness in banks and savings and loan advertising. &nbsp;Technology advertising, which represented 17% of total U.S. Journal linage, fell 23.8% due to softness in nearly all technology categories. &nbsp;Classified and other advertising linage, which represented about 24% of total U.S. Journal linage, increased 8.9% while ad revenue increased about 12%, driven by strong increases in real estate advertising coupled with increases in classified advertising. &nbsp;Color advertising pages increased 20%, and color premium revenue was up 34%. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>23</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Circulation and other revenue for U.S. print publications decreased $2.9 million, or 1.1%, to $260.4 million in part due to lower contractual printing for third parties and slightly lower circulation revenue reflecting somewhat more discounted rates. &nbsp;Average circulation for 2004 for <I>The Wall Street Journal</I> was 1,810,000 compared with circulation of 1,792,000 in 2003. &nbsp;<I>Barron&#146;s</I> average circulation was 299,000 in 2004 compared with 297,000 in 2003.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>International Publications:<I> </I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Revenues at our international publications were flat, as revenue increases at the international editions of the Journal were offset by revenue declines at the <I>Far Eastern Economic Review</I> (FEER), largely due to repositioning of their operations in the fourth quarter of 2004 from a weekly magazine to a monthly publication. &nbsp;International print publication advertising revenues increased $1 million, or 2%, to $48.6 million, as gains in advertising rates were partially offset by a decrease in advertising volume at <I>The Wall Street Journal</I> <I>Asia </I>and <I>The Wall Street Journal Europe</I> and the lower revenue from FEER. &nbsp;International print circulation and other revenues decreased $1 million, or 2.8%, to $33.2 million, in part due to lower conferences revenue and circulation revenue at FEER. &nbsp;Combined average circulation for the International Journals was 167,000 in 2004 compared with 168,000 in 2003.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify> <BR>
</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Expenses</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Print publishing expenses in 2004 were held to a $10 million, or 1.1%, increase to $917.3 million, as modest growth in employee compensation and higher newsprint costs were mitigated by lower costs related to the repositioning of FEER operations and lower depreciation expense. &nbsp;Newsprint expense was up 8% as a result of a 6% increase in newsprint prices coupled with a 1.9% increase in consumption. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I> <BR>
</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Income</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Print publishing operating income in 2004 was $31.5 million (3.3% of revenues) an improvement of $23.4 million compared with operating income of $8.1 million (0.9% of revenues) in 2003 as increased profits at the U.S. Journal and U.S television were partially offset by higher losses overseas, in part due to unfavorable foreign currency translation costs. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Electronic Publishing </B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Electronic publishing, which electronically distributes business and financial news and information, includes the operations of Dow Jones Newswires, Consumer Electronic Publishing and Dow Jones Indexes/Ventures. &nbsp;Consumer Electronic Publishing includes the results of <I>WSJ.com</I> and its related vertical sites, MarketWatch and the Company&#146;s licensing, business development and radio/audio businesses. &nbsp;The Company manages electronic publishing as one segment, based on the similar distribution channels, global management, shared workforce and corporate branding. &nbsp;Revenues in the electronic publishing segment are mainly subscription-based but also include online advertising and other revenues.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>On January 21, 2005, the Company completed the acquisition of MarketWatch for a purchase price of $532 million, including certain transaction costs. &nbsp;The Company fully integrated MarketWatch into the Consumer Electronic Publishing business. &nbsp;On July 7, 2004, the Company acquired the remaining two-thirds interest in OsterDow Jones Commodity News for $1.6 million. &nbsp;On April 2, 2004, the Company acquired the remaining interest in the news operations of Vereinigte Wirtschaftsdienste GmbH (VWD), a German newswires business, for $12.1 million. &nbsp;The acquired business consists of financial newswires and newsletters. &nbsp;The Company was a minority shareholder in VWD. &nbsp;On March 19, 2004, the Company purchased Alternative Investor, a provider of newsletters, databases and industry conferences for the venture capital and private equity markets for $85 million. &nbsp;All of the above acquisitions, excluding MarketWatch, are now part of Dow Jones Newswires.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><U><BR></U></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I><U><BR></U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Electronic publishing revenues increased $125.7 million, or 33%, to $506.9 million, driven by acquisitions and strong organic revenue growth at all electronic publishing businesses. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Dow Jones Newswires revenue increased $19.7 million, or 8%, to $267.8 million (up 3.8% excluding acquisitions made during 2004). Revenues in North America increased 4% and internationally increased 21%, driven almost entirely by acquisitions. &nbsp;The number of English-language terminals carrying Dow Jones Newswires at December 31, 2005 was 304,000, an increase of 6,000 compared to last year as an increase of 10,000 terminals internationally was partially offset by a 4,000 terminal decrease in North America.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Consumer Electronic Publishing revenue increased $93 million, or 117%, to $172.7 million, primarily driven by the MarketWatch acquisition and strong revenue growth at <I>WSJ.com</I>. &nbsp;On a pro forma basis, including MarketWatch revenues in the respective periods prior to the Company&#146;s acquisition in January 2005, Consumer Electronic Publishing revenues grew 10.2%, reflecting growth in advertising and subscriber revenue. &nbsp;The <I>WSJ.com</I> Web site continued to be the largest paid subscription news site on the Internet with subscribers of 768,000 as of December 31, 2005 compared to 712,000 a year earlier, while also increasing the subscription price during 2005. &nbsp;Including MarketWatch, total unduplicated unique visitors and page views to the <I>Dow Jones Online Network</I> averaged approximately 8 million and 299 million, respectively, per month during the fourth quarter of 2005.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Dow Jones Indexes/Ventures revenues, which include Dow Jones Indexes and reprints/permissions businesses, increased $13 million, or 24.3%, to $66.4 million from continued growth in the number of licensees and indexes published.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>25</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Expenses </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Electronic publishing expenses were up $92.7 million, or 30.7%, to $394.8 million, largely due to acquisitions in 2004 and 2005, with the remainder of the increase primarily from higher compensation, facilities and marketing costs. &nbsp;The number of full-time employees in the electronic publishing segment was up 18% from a year ago mainly due to acquisitions.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Income </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Electronic publishing&#146;s operating income was $112 million (22.1% of revenues), an improvement of $33 million, or 41.8%, over 2004 operating income $79 million (20.7% of revenues), driven by increased profits at Consumer Electronic Publishing and Dow Jones Indexes/Ventures. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I><U><BR></U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I><U><BR></U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I><U><BR></U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Electronic publishing revenues in 2004 increased $59.1 million, or 18%, to $381.2 million, primarily as a result of business acquisitions at Dow Jones Newswires and revenue gains at Dow Jones Indexes/Ventures and Consumer Electronic Publishing. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Dow Jones Newswires revenue increased $35 million, or 16%, to $248.1 million, due to recent acquisitions. &nbsp;Excluding recent acquisitions, Dow Jones Newswires revenues were relatively flat. &nbsp;English-language terminals carrying Dow Jones Newswires at December 31, 2004, were 298,000 compared with 293,000 at December 31, 2003. &nbsp;North American terminals increased by 1,000 and International terminals increased by 4,000. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Consumer Electronic Publishing revenue increased $11 million, or 16%, to $79.7 million on a 26% increase in advertising revenue coupled with increases in licensing revenue and <I>WSJ.com</I> subscriber revenue. &nbsp;At the end of December 2004, the number of <I>WSJ.com</I> subscribers reached 712,000, an increase of 3.3% from a year earlier. &nbsp;Dow Jones Indexes/Ventures revenues, which include Dow Jones Indexes and reprints/permissions businesses, increased $13.2 million, or 33%, to $53.4 million, driven by increases in Indexes revenue and in reprints and permissions revenue.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify> <BR>
</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Expenses</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Electronic publishing expenses were up $48 million, or 19%, to $302.1 million, primarily as a result of incremental expenses from recent acquisitions (comprising nearly two thirds of the increase) as well as an increase in employee compensation.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>26</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Income</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Electronic publishing&#146;s operating income was $79 million (20.7% of revenues), an improvement of $11.2 million, or 16%, over 2003 operating income of $67.9 million (21.1% of revenues). &nbsp;The improvement was driven by increased profits at Consumer Electronic Publishing, Dow Jones Indexes/Ventures and from recent acquisitions.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Community Newspapers</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Our Ottaway community newspapers segment publishes 15 daily newspapers and over 30 weekly newspapers and &#147;shoppers&#148; in nine states in the U.S. &nbsp;Ottaway serves relatively small, self-contained communities, outside the heavy competitive pressures of large metropolitan papers and other media. &nbsp;Ottaway&#146;s strong and stable cash flow over the years has helped us weather a particularly harsh B2B ad environment in our print publishing segment. &nbsp;During 2005, Ottaway&#146;s revenue grew modestly over 2004 but operating income declined as we invested in a new Ottaway-wide internet initiative and content management system to help drive continued increases in Ottaway&#146;s internet ad revenues.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Community newspaper revenue was up $5.3 million, or 1.5%, to $346.7 million on a 2.4% increase in advertising revenue as a 2.6% decline in overall linage was more than offset by higher advertising rates and preprint revenue as well as a 30% increase in internet advertising revenues. &nbsp;The decline in advertising linage primarily reflected double digit declines in auto classified advertising, which exceeded the gains in real estate classified advertising. &nbsp;Average daily circulation in 2005 was approximately 431,000 compared with 436,000 in 2004.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Expenses </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Community newspaper expenses increased $14.6 million, or 5.8%, to $266.9 million as a result of higher compensation, marketing, and newsprint expenses. &nbsp;Expenses in 2005 also included increased costs from a new Ottaway-wide Internet initiative and content management system, which will contribute to increased online advertising revenue and profit in the future. &nbsp;Newsprint expense increased 7.7% as a result of a 10.6% increase in newsprint prices, which was partially offset by a 2.7% decrease in consumption. &nbsp;The number of full-time employees in the community newspapers segment increased 2% as compared to last year. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Income </U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Operating income in 2005 was $79.7 million (23.0% of revenues) compared with income last year of $89.1 million (26.1% of revenues). </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><BR></P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:36pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Revenues</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Community newspapers 2004 revenue was up $30.5 million, or 9.8%, to $341.4 million reflecting in part newly-acquired properties. &nbsp;On a same property basis, revenue increased $17.5 million, or 5.7%. &nbsp;Same property advertising revenue increased $17.4 million, or 7.7%, to $242.2 million, primarily reflecting an increase in advertising linage, as well as average advertising rates and preprint revenue. &nbsp;Same property circulation and other revenue increased slightly, to $83.2 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U> <BR>
</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Expenses</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Community newspapers expenses in 2004 increased $22.3 million, or 9.7%, to $252.3 million, partially reflecting newly acquired properties. &nbsp;On a same property basis, expenses increased $12.4 million, or 5.5%, as a result of increases in compensation expense, newsprint and outside service costs. &nbsp;Newsprint expense, on a same property basis, increased 10.2% as a result of an 8.2% increase in newsprint prices coupled with an increase in consumption of 1.8%.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify> <BR>
</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><U>Operating Income</U></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; padding-right:25.2pt; width:532.8pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Community newspapers operating income in 2004 was $89.1 million (26.1% of revenues) compared with 2003 operating income of $81 million (26.0% of revenues). &nbsp;On a same property basis, 2004 operating income of $85.3 million (26.2% of revenues) increased 6.3% from $80.2 million (26.1% of revenues) in 2003.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; padding-right:1.8pt; width:556.2pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
