<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U>(a) Restructuring and other items:</U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><BR></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2005</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In the second quarter of 2005, the Company recorded a restructuring charge of $11.4 million ($6.9 million, net of taxes) primarily reflecting employee severance related to a workforce reduction of about 120 full-time employees. &nbsp;Most of the charge related to the Company&#146;s efforts to reposition its international print and online operations but also included headcount reductions at other parts of the business. &nbsp;These workforce reductions were substantially completed by the end of the year. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2004</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>During 2004, the Company recorded a net charge of $3.9 million ($2.3 million, net of taxes) reflecting a restructuring charge of $6.7 million for workforce reductions partially offset by a reversal of a $2.8 million reserve related to an office lease. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The restructuring charge of $6.7 million ($4.0 million, net of taxes) primarily reflected employee severance related to a workforce reduction of about 100 employees in connection with the Company&#146;s decision to publish FEER as a monthly periodical beginning in December 2004, with the balance of the charge related to headcount reductions in circulation and international operations. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>On September 11, 2001, the Company&#146;s headquarters at the World Financial Center (WFC) sustained damage from debris and dust as a result of the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center. &nbsp;Approximately 60% of the floor space, including furniture and related equipment, had been determined a total loss. &nbsp;In the fourth quarter 2001, the Company recorded a charge of $32.2 million as a result of its decision to permanently re-deploy certain personnel and to abandon four of seven floors that were leased at its World Financial Center headquarters. &nbsp;This charge primarily reflected the Company&#146;s rent obligation through May 2005 on this vacated space. &nbsp;In the first quarter of 2004, the Company decided to extend the term of its lease for one of the floors that was previously abandoned and reoccupy this floor with personnel from another of its New York locations, whose lease term was expiring. &nbsp;As a result, the Company reversed $2.8 million ($1.7 million, net of taxes) of the remaining lease obligation reserve for the previously abandoned floor at WFC.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2003</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company has insurance policies that cover property damage, extra expenses and business interruption related to the September 11 disaster. &nbsp;In the second quarter of 2003, the Company recorded a gain of $18.4 million ($11.1 million, net of taxes) reflecting the settlement of its business interruption insurance claim for loss of operating income suffered as a result of the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>See Note 4 for additional information on restructuring. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U><BR>
<BR></U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>29</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U>(b) Contract guarantee: </U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Under the terms of the Company's 1998 sale of Telerate to Bridge Information Systems (Bridge), the Company retained its guarantee of payments under certain circumstances of certain minimum payments for data acquired by Telerate from Cantor Fitzgerald Securities (Cantor) and Market Data Corporation (MDC). &nbsp;The annual minimum payments average approximately $50 million per year through October 2006 under certain conditions. &nbsp;Bridge agreed to indemnify the Company for any liability the Company incurred under the contract guarantee with respect to periods subsequent to Bridge's purchase of Telerate. &nbsp;In 2000, based in part on uncertainty with Bridge's solvency as well as other factors, the Company established a reserve of $255 million representing the present value of the total estimated minimum annual payments of about $300 million from 2001 through October 2006, using a discount rate of approximately 6%. &nbsp;Bridge filed for bankruptcy in February 2001, but made payments for this data for the post-petition periods through October 2001, when Telerate ceased operations, went out of business, sold certain assets and rejected its contracts with Cantor and MDC. &nbsp;The Company is now in litigation with Cantor and MDC with respect to their claims for amounts due under the contract guarantee. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company has various substantial defenses to these claims and the litigation is proceeding. &nbsp;The trial court in January 2003 denied motions by each of the parties that their own claims for relief be granted and that competing claims be dismissed. &nbsp;Appeals from those decisions were not pursued, and discovery has concluded. &nbsp;On January 25, 2006, the trial court denied the bulk of the parties' motions for summary judgment, leaving the resolution of the case for trial. &nbsp;The Court did grant Dow Jones' motion for summary judgment on a small issue in the case. &nbsp;The Court did not set a trial date, but has directed the parties to appear before it at a settlement conference in early March 2006.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Earnings in 2005, 2004 and 2003 included accretion charges of $4.1 million, $6.9 million and $9.5 million, respectively, which increased the reserve balance as of December 31, 2005 to $264.7 million, all of which is classified as current based on the original due dates of the contract. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U><BR></U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U>(c) Gain on disposition of investments:</U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2005</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In April 2005, the Company concluded the sale of its 39.9% minority interest in F.F. Soucy Inc., a Canadian newsprint mill, to its majority owner, Brant-Allen Industries, Inc. &nbsp;The proceeds from the sale price of $40 million in cash were used to reduce the Company&#146;s commercial paper borrowings. &nbsp;The Company recorded a gain of $9.6 million ($9.4 million, net of taxes) in the second quarter.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>During the second quarter of 2005, the Company and the von Holtzbrinck Group completed its exchange of cross shareholdings. &nbsp;In exchange for the Company&#146;s 10% interest in <I>Handelsblatt</I>, the Company received the remaining 10% minority interest in <I>The Wall Street Journal Europe</I> that it did not already own; an 11.5% increase in its interest in a Czech Republic business periodical, effectively increasing the Company&#146;s interest to 23%; and $6 million in cash. &nbsp;The transaction was accounted for at fair value in accordance with EITF 01-2, <I>Interpretations of APB 29</I>, and the Company recorded a gain of $13.2 million ($8.3 million, net of taxes) in connection with the disposal of its interest in <I>Handelsblatt</I>.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2004</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In April 2004, simultaneous with the Company&#146;s acquisition of the remaining interest in the news operations of Vereinigte Wirtschaftsdienste GmbH (VWD), VWD sold its non-news assets to a third party, resulting in cash proceeds to the Company of $6.7 million. &nbsp;As a result of this sale, the Company recorded a gain of $3.3 million ($1.8 million, net of taxes) in the second quarter of 2004. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2003</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In December 2003, the Company and the von Holtzbrinck Group exchanged equity shareholdings so as to increase the Company's ownership of <I>The Wall Street Journal Europe</I> to 90% from 51% and reduce the Company&#146;s ownership of the von Holtzbrinck Group&#146;s business daily, <I>Handelsblatt</I>, to 10% from 22%, with news and advertising relationships continuing. &nbsp;The transaction was accounted for at fair value in accordance with EITF 01-2 as a disposition of 12% of <I>Handelsblatt</I> in exchange for the acquisition of an additional 39% interest in <I>The Wall Street Journal Europe</I>. &nbsp;The Company recorded a gain of $18.7 million ($11.4 million after taxes), on the disposal of the 12% interest in <I>Handelsblatt</I>, as the risks of ownership were relinquished at the time of sale. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>30</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U>(d) Gain on resolution of Telerate sale loss contingencies:</U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U><BR></U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In the first quarter of 2003, the Company recorded a gain of $59.8 million on the resolution of certain loss contingencies resulting from the sale of its former Telerate subsidiary to Bridge Information Systems. &nbsp;The reserve for loss contingencies was established as part of the loss on the sale of Telerate in 1998 and related to various claims that arose out of the Stock Purchase Agreement, including a purchase price adjustment related to working capital, an indemnification undertaking and other actual and potential claims and counter-claims between the Company and Bridge. &nbsp;In February 2001, Bridge declared bankruptcy. &nbsp;In March 2003, these matters were resolved by the bankruptcy court, and the Company&#146;s contingent liabilities were thereby extinguished.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U>(e) Write-down of equity investments:</U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In December 2005, the Company completed the disposal of its 50% interests in both CNBC Europe and CNBC Asia (collectively CNBC International), as well as its 25% interest in CNBC World, to NBC Universal for nominal consideration pursuant to a July 2005 agreement. &nbsp;Through 2006 the Company will continue to provide access to news resources and other services to CNBC International, nonexclusively. &nbsp;There are no plans to alter the licensing relationship in the U.S. between the Company and CNBC.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In the second quarter of 2005, in connection with the binding agreement reached with NBC Universal, the Company determined that an other-than-temporary decline in the value of its investments in CNBC International and CNBC World had occurred and, as a result, the Company recorded a charge of $35.9 million ($36.7 million, including taxes), largely reflecting the write-down of the investments&#146; carrying value ($32 million), with the remainder primarily reflecting the additional firmly committed cash payment for which there was no future economic benefit to the Company.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><BR></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U>(f) Restructuring by an equity investment: </U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>During the fourth quarter 2005, Dow Jones Reuters Business Interactive LLC (Factiva), a 50% equity investment, recorded a restructuring charge of $4.3 million primarily reflecting employee severance and termination of an operating lease. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s share of this restructuring charge was $2.1 million ($1.3 million, net of taxes). </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><U>(g) Resolution of certain income tax matters:</U></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2005</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In the fourth quarter 2005, the Company received a federal tax refund, including interest, related to the settlement of claims from previously filed returns. &nbsp;Pursuant to the settlement of these claims, during the fourth quarter of 2005, the Company recorded an adjustment of $8 million to its tax accounts and recorded interest income of $1.4 million ($0.9 million, net of taxes). &nbsp;The total impact of these items was an increase in net income of $8.9 million. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Income tax expense in the third quarter 2005 included a tax benefit of $1.1 million as a result of a favorable resolution of certain state and federal tax matters.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2004</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Income tax expense in 2004 included tax benefits of $5.7 million in the fourth quarter and $1.5 million in the third quarter as a result of the favorable resolution of certain federal tax matters. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><BR></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>2003</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In the third quarter of 2003, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) completed its audit of the Company&#146;s tax returns for the 1995 through 1998 tax periods, which had been amended for additional tax refunds. &nbsp;In October 2003, the Company received notification that the Congressional Joint Committee on Taxation had approved these claims for tax refunds of approximately $24 million. &nbsp;The Company received these refunds plus interest of approximately $6.7 million in the fourth quarter of 2003. &nbsp;Pursuant to the settlement of these claims, in the third quarter of 2003, the Company recorded an adjustment of $25 million to its tax reserve balance as a result of the resolution of certain tax matters and recorded interest income of $6.7 million ($4.0 million, net of taxes). &nbsp;The Company also recorded a provision of $9.5 million in the third quarter for loss contingencies relating to recent developments in certain other tax matters. &nbsp;The net effect of these items was an increase in net income of $19.5 million. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><BR></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><BR></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B><BR>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Capital Loss Carryforward</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>As of December 31, 2005, the Company had a capital loss carryforward remaining of about $454 million (a deferred tax asset of about $170 million, with a full valuation allowance). &nbsp;Approximately $164 million of this loss carryforward is recognized for tax purposes, the bulk of which expires in 2006. &nbsp;The remaining $290 million of capital loss carryforward, which primarily relates to the contract guarantee obligation, will be recognized for tax purposes only to the extent, if any, that the Company is required to make payment. &nbsp;If the Company is required to make any such payment, the resulting loss carryforward will be available for use five years from the year it is recognized.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Net Operating Loss Carryforward- acquired</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>As part of the MarketWatch acquisition, the Company acquired a net operating loss carryforward of approximately $110.7 million (a deferred tax asset of about $42.8 million). &nbsp;Approximately $16.8 million of this loss carryforward (or $6.2 million of tax benefit) was utilized in 2005. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, the remaining loss carryforward, which is subject to annual limitations of its use, was $93.9 million (a deferred tax asset of about $36.6 million).</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><BR></P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>32</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Liquidity and Capital Resources </B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Overview</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The primary source of the Company&#146;s liquidity is cash flow from operating activities.&nbsp; The key component of operating cash inflow is cash receipts from advertising customers and subscribers to print publications and electronic information services. &nbsp;Operating cash outflows include payments to vendors for raw materials, services and supplies, payments to employees, and payments of interest and income taxes. Certain employee compensation, such as bonuses and payments to the Company&#146;s defined contribution pension plan, are paid annually in the first quarter of the year. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>As previously disclosed, in 2000 the Company established a reserve for the present value of the total estimated payments through October 2006 in connection with the Company&#146;s guarantee of certain minimum payments for data acquired by the Company&#146;s former Telerate subsidiary from Cantor Fitzgerald Securities (Cantor) and Market Data Corporation (MDC). &nbsp;Bridge Information Systems, Inc., which purchased Telerate in 1998, filed for bankruptcy but made payments for this data for the post-petition periods through October 2001, when Telerate ceased operations, went out of business, sold certain assets and rejected its contracts with Cantor and MDC. &nbsp;The Company is now in litigation with Cantor and MDC with respect to their claims for amounts allegedly due under the contract guarantee. &nbsp;The Company has various substantial defenses to these claims and the litigation is proceeding. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>As of December 31, 2005, the reserve for the contract guarantee was $264.7 million, all of which is classified as current based on the original due dates of the contract. &nbsp;Due to the stage of the lawsuit at December 31, 2005, it is not possible to determine whether the court will find that any obligation under the guarantee may be dismissed or reduced. &nbsp;Accordingly, the Company believes the balance of the reserve continues to be appropriate. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I><BR></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company&#146;s liquidity requirements may be funded, if necessary, through the issuance of commercial paper, bank loans or debt securities. &nbsp;Debt outstanding at December 31, 2005 was $472.4 million which consisted of 3-year bonds totaling $224.9 million and commercial paper of $247.5 million with various maturities of less than a year. &nbsp;It is currently the Company&#146;s intent to manage its commercial paper borrowings as short-term obligations. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s commercial paper program is supported by multiyear revolving credit facilities with several banks. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, the Company could borrow up to $440 million, $140 million through June 24, 2006 and $300 million through June 24, 2009 under its multiyear revolving credit agreements with several banks. &nbsp;The Company intends to renew the revolving credit line set to expire on June 24, 2006. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The revolving credit agreements contain restrictive covenants, including a limitation on the ratio of consolidated indebtedness to consolidated cash flow and a requirement to maintain a minimum ratio of consolidated cash flow to consolidated interest expense. &nbsp;On August 29, 2005, the Company amended its 5-year credit agreement dated June 25, 2001 and its 5-year credit agreement dated June 21, 2004 to temporarily increase the leverage covenant, from 3.5x to 4.0x, for each of the two quarters ended September 30, 2005 and December 31, 2005. &nbsp;At December 31, 2005, the Company was in compliance with respect to both of these restrictive covenants then in effect, with the actual leverage ratio equaling less than 3.0x. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s original restrictive covenants will be effective for periods subsequent to December 31, 2005.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Future Liquidity and Capital Resources Requirements</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In 2006, the Company expects its beginning cash balance and cash provided by operations to be sufficient to meet its recurring operating commitments, fund capital expenditures of about $100 million, including $36 million related to the reconfiguration of presses for the previously announced web-width reduction initiative, and pay dividends. &nbsp;After funding capital expenditures and dividends, the Company anticipates that remaining excess cash flow from operations will be used to reduce and service its debt. &nbsp;As previously disclosed, litigation with Cantor and MDC with respect to their claim for amounts allegedly due under the contract guarantee is proceeding. &nbsp;In the event there is an adverse judgment against the Company it would likely be appealed. &nbsp;If any significant amounts are ultimately considered due, they would likely be financed through the issuance of additional debt.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Credit Ratings</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>On February 8, 2006, Standard &amp; Poor&#146;s (S&amp;P), a credit ratings agency, lowered the Company&#146;s long-term corporate credit and senior unsecured credit ratings by one notch from A- to BBB+ and cited the volatility in print publishing advertising revenue, and therefore cash flow, as the key driver for the action. &nbsp;This resolves the &#147;CreditWatch&#148; S&amp;P placed on the Company on October 21, 2005. &nbsp;At the same time, however, the Company&#146;s short-term corporate credit and commercial paper ratings were affirmed by S&amp;P. &nbsp;The downgrade to the Company&#146;s long-term credit ratings by S&amp;P is not expected to significantly affect the Company&#146;s borrowing costs. &nbsp;On February 3, 2006, Moody&#146;s Investors Service (Moody&#146;s), another credit ratings agency, indicated that the Company&#146;s senior unsecured debt and commercial paper ratings are under review for possible downgrade. &nbsp;On November 14, 2005, Fitch Ratings (Fitch), another credit ratings agency, downgraded by one notch the Company&#146;s senior unsecured debt and commercial-paper ratings. &nbsp;Concurrently, Fitch noted that the rating outlook for the Company is stable.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Operating Activities</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Cash provided by operating activities for 2005 was $197.5 million, which was down $54.4 million, or 21.6%, from net cash provided by operations last year. &nbsp;The decline was primarily the result of lower operating income at print publishing coupled with higher interest costs related to the acquisition of MarketWatch in January 2005.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Cash provided by operating activities in 2004 was $251.9 million, which was up $31.6 million, or 14.3%, from net cash provided by operations in 2003, primarily due to higher operating income and increases in cash as a result of changes in working capital reflecting higher subscriptions received and lower payments related to employee benefits offset by higher income taxes paid in 2004 relative to 2003.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Investing Activities</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Net cash used in investing activities was $472.5 million in 2005, primarily as a result of the January 21, 2005 acquisition of MarketWatch as well as capital expenditures of $65.3 million. &nbsp;Partially offsetting those outflows were cash receipts of approximately $40 million from the sale of the Company&#146;s interest in F.F. Soucy, Inc. as well as approximately $6 million from the exchange of cross shareholdings between the Company and the von Holtzbrinck Group.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Net cash used in investing activities was $174.4 million in 2004, which reflected business acquisitions totaling $98 million (primarily Alternative Investor for $85 million) and capital expenditures of $76 million. &nbsp;Net cash used in investing activities was $216 million in 2003 which primarily reflected the $146 million acquisition of <I>The Record of Stockton, California</I>, capital expenditures of $55.9 million and the funding of equity investments. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Financing Activities</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Net cash provided by financing activities in 2005 was $268 million, primarily reflecting proceeds from the issuance of debt ($439 million) to finance the January 2005 MarketWatch acquisition and proceeds from sales under stock compensation plans of $23.5 million. &nbsp;Cash outlays in 2005 included the subsequent repayment of borrowings as well as the payment of $82.7 million in dividends to shareholders. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Net cash used in financing activities in 2004 was $82.2 million, including the payment of $81.8 million in dividends to shareholders, and a net decrease in debt of $7.3 million partially offset by proceeds from sales under stock compensation plans of $11.4 million. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Net cash used in financing activities in 2003 was $19.8 million. &nbsp;Cash outlays in 2003 included the payment of $81.6 million in dividends to shareholders and the repurchase of shares of treasury stock of $21 million. &nbsp;Sources of cash from financing activities in 2003 included a net increase in debt of $65 million, proceeds from sales under stock compensation plans of $12 million, as well as the receipt of $7 million from a minority shareholder to fund a subsidiary, net of distributions. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Critical Accounting Estimates</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company's discussion and analysis of its financial condition and results of operations are based upon the Company's consolidated financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. &nbsp;The preparation of these financial statements requires the Company's management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses, and related disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities. &nbsp;The accounting estimates and assumptions discussed in this section are those that the Company considers to be important to understanding the Company&#146;s financial statements because they inherently involve significant judgments and estimates on the part of management. &nbsp;Actual results may differ from estimates.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Revenue Recognition</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Advertising revenue, net of commissions, is recognized in the period in which the advertisement is displayed. &nbsp;The Company's advertising rate card reflects certain volume-based discounts and certain customers also qualify for volume-based bonus advertisements. &nbsp;These programs require management to make certain estimates regarding future advertising volume. &nbsp;The estimated rebates and bonus advertisements are recorded as reductions of revenue in the periods the advertisements are displayed and are revised as necessary based on actual volume realized. &nbsp;For the years ended December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003, the Company&#146;s estimated rebate and bonus advertising reserves totaled $15.5 million, $8.5 million and $12.4 million, respectively and were classified as a liability. &nbsp;Certain online-related advertising revenues are based on the number of &quot;impressions&#148; delivered and are recognized as impressions occur, while other online advertising revenues are based on a fixed duration campaign and are recognized ratably over the term of the campaign.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Revenue recognition from subscriptions to the Company's print publications and information services is recognized in income as earned, pro rata on a per-issue basis, over the subscription period. &nbsp;Circulation revenue includes sales to retail outlets/newsstands, which are subject to returns. &nbsp;The Company records these retail sales upon delivery, net of estimated returns. &nbsp;These estimated returns are based on historical return rates and are revised as necessary based on actual returns experienced. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s estimated returns reserves totaled approximately $3 million for each of the years ended December 31, 2005, 2004 and 2003. &nbsp;Costs in connection with the procurement of subscriptions are charged to expense as incurred. &nbsp;Revenue from licensing the Dow Jones Averages includes both upfront one-time fees and ongoing revenue. &nbsp;Both upfront fees and ongoing licensing revenue are recognized in income as earned over the license period.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Allowance for Doubtful Accounts</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Accounts receivable includes an allowance for doubtful accounts, which is an estimate of amounts that may not be collectible. &nbsp;This estimated allowance is based on historical trends, review of aging categories and the specific identification of certain customers that are at risk of not paying. &nbsp;Actual write-offs of bad debt have historically been insignificant, less than 0.5% of revenues.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Pensions and Other Postretirement Benefits</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Certain costs and related obligations of the Company are based on actuarial assumptions, including some of its pension plans and the cost of the Company&#146;s postretirement medical plan, which provides lifetime health care benefits to retirees who meet specified length of service and age requirements. &nbsp;These benefit costs are expensed over the employee&#146;s expected employment period. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>At December 31, 2005, the Company&#146;s postretirement retiree medical benefit obligation was $261.2 million, which is not funded as it is the Company&#146;s policy to fund postretirement medical costs as claims are incurred. &nbsp;In determining the cost of retiree medical costs, some factors that management must consider include the expected increase in health care costs, discount rates and turnover and mortality rates, which are updated periodically based on recent actual trends. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s discount rate was determined by projecting the plans&#146; expected future benefit payments, as defined for the projected benefit obligations, and discounting those expected payments using an average of yield curves constructed of a large population of high-quality corporate bonds. &nbsp;The resulting discount rate reflects the matching of plan liability cash flows to the yield curves. &nbsp;Increasing the assumed health care cost trend rates by one percentage point in each year would have increased the accumulated postretirement benefit obligation by $48.2 million and the cost for 2005 by $5.7 million. &nbsp;Conversely, a one percentage point decline in assumed health care cost trend rates would have lowered the benefit obligation at the end of 2005 by $40.3 million and the cost for 2005 by $4.5 million. &nbsp;A one quarter of one percentage point decrease in the Company's expected discount rate in 2005 would have increased retiree medical expense by approximately $1 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>36</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The majority of the Company&#146;s employees who meet specific length of service requirements are covered by defined contribution retirement plans, which are funded currently. &nbsp;Substantially all employees who are not covered by these plans are covered by defined benefit pension plans based on length of service and age requirements. &nbsp;At December 31, 2005, the Company&#146;s accumulated pension benefit obligation was $193.8 million, of which $157.7 million was funded. &nbsp;In determining the cost and obligation of the defined pension benefit plans, management must consider such factors as the expected return on plan assets, discount rates, mortality rates and expected employee salary increases. &nbsp;While the Company believes its assumptions are appropriate, significant differences in actual experience or changes in these assumptions would affect the calculation of its projected obligation and cost under the defined benefit pension and postretirement medical plans. &nbsp;The Company evaluates its actuarial assumptions annually. &nbsp;A one quarter of one percentage point decrease in the expected discount rate on the Company&#146;s defined benefit pension plans in 2005 would have increased pension expense by approximately $0.5 million. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Long-lived Assets</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Management must use its judgment in assessing whether the carrying value of certain long-lived assets, cost-method investments, identifiable intangibles and goodwill is impaired and if any asset is impaired, the extent of any such loss. &nbsp;Certain events or changes in circumstances may indicate that the carrying value may not be recoverable and require an impairment review. &nbsp;Based on that review, if the carrying value of these assets exceeds fair value and is determined to not be recoverable, an impairment loss representing the amount of excess over its fair value would be recognized in income. &nbsp;Fair value estimates are based on quoted market values in active markets, if available. &nbsp;If quoted market prices are not available, the estimate of fair value is based on various valuation techniques, including discounted value of estimated future cash flows. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Management also exercises judgment in determining the estimated useful life of long-lived assets, specifically plant, property and equipment and certain intangible assets with a finite life. &nbsp;The Company depreciates the cost of buildings over 40 years; improvements to the buildings over 10 years; software over 3 to 5 years and machinery and equipment over 3 to 25 years. &nbsp;The 25-year life is applicable to the Company&#146;s press equipment. &nbsp;The cost of leasehold improvements is depreciated over the lesser of the useful lives or the terms of the respective leases. &nbsp;Management bases its judgment on estimated lives of these assets based on actual experienced length of service of similar assets and expert opinions. &nbsp;The Company also obtains third party appraisals to assist in determining whether an intangible asset has an indefinite life.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:9pt" align=justify><I><BR></I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Stock Based Compensation</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company maintains a stock incentive plan under the Dow Jones 2001 Long-Term Incentive Plan. &nbsp;This plan provides for the grant of contingent stock rights, stock options, restricted stock, restricted stock units and other stock-based awards. &nbsp;The Company accounts for its stock-based compensation in accordance with APB 25 and its related interpretations. &nbsp;Under APB 25, pretax stock-based compensation charged to income principally in relation to the Company&#146;s contingent stock rights, restricted stock units and restricted stock awards was $10 million in 2005, $8.7 million in 2004 and $7.4 million in 2003. &nbsp;Had the Company&#146;s stock-based compensation been determined by the fair-value based method of SFAS 123, &#147;<I>Accounting for Stock-Based Compensation,</I>&#148; the Company&#146;s earnings per share for 2005, 2004 and 2003 would have been reduced by approximately $.03 per share, $.27 per share and $.19 per share, respectively. &nbsp;See Notes 1 and 12 for additional details on our stock compensation plans. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Contingencies</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Management must exercise judgment in assessing the likely outcome of contingencies including those relating to tax matters, legal proceedings and other matters that have arisen in the ordinary course of business and those described in Note 7 to the financial statements. &nbsp;Both the timing and amount of the provisions made in the financial statements and related disclosures represent management's judgment of likelihood, based on information available at the time and on the advice of legal counsel. &nbsp;Judicial or governmental bodies largely determine the outcome of these matters. &nbsp;With regard to tax matters, the ultimate resolution of these matters, either by determinations by these bodies or other means, could be materially different from that assumed by the Company in making its provisions and related disclosures. &nbsp;At the time that these tax contingencies are resolved by tax examination or the expiration of the statute of limitations, the Company adjusts its tax accounts accordingly.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Tax Valuation Allowance</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company records a tax valuation allowance to reduce its deferred tax assets to the amount that is more likely than not to be realized. &nbsp;Currently, the Company maintains a valuation allowance on deferred tax assets related to its capital loss carryforward. &nbsp;The Company has considered ongoing prudent and feasible tax planning strategies in assessing the need for a valuation allowance. &nbsp;In the event the Company were to determine that it would be able to realize all or a portion of its net deferred tax assets, an adjustment to the deferred tax asset valuation allowance would increase income in the period such determination was made. &nbsp;Likewise, should the Company subsequently determine that it would not be able to realize all or a portion of its net deferred tax asset in the future, an adjustment to the deferred tax asset valuation allowance would be charged to income in the period such determination was made. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=center>37</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:48.25pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:563.75pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:12pt"><BR></P>
<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>Recent Accounting Pronouncements</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In December 2004, the FASB issued Statement of Financial Accounting Standards No. 123 (revised 2004), &quot;<I>Share-Based Payment</I>&quot; (SFAS 123R). &nbsp;This statement eliminated the alternative to apply the intrinsic value measurement provisions of Accounting Principles Board Opinion No.&nbsp;25, &quot;<I>Accounting for Stock Issued to Employees</I>&#148; to stock compensation awards issued to employees. &nbsp;Rather, SFAS 123R requires companies to measure the cost of employee services received in exchange for an award of equity instruments based on the grant-date fair value of the award. &nbsp;That cost will be recognized in the consolidated statement of income over the period during which an employee is required to provide services in exchange for the award, usually the vesting period. &nbsp;The Company plans to adopt SFAS 123R and the related FASB Staff Positions using the modified prospective application, one of several alternative transition methods, when it is effective for the Company on January 1, 2006. &nbsp;Management estimates that the adoption of SFAS 123R will result in additional expense of approximately $.04 per diluted share during 2006.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company also enters into foreign currency exchange forward contracts to limit the cash flow and earnings volatility that results from remeasuring certain foreign currency payables at prevailing exchange rates. &nbsp;The unrealized gains or losses of these forward contracts are recognized in Other, net in the income statement. &nbsp;The forward contract acts as an economic hedge by increasing in value when the underlying foreign currency payable decreases in value and conversely decreases in value when the underlying foreign currency payable increases. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2005, the Company had forward currency exchange contracts outstanding to exchange 10 million British Pounds for $17.2 million, which are due to expire in the first quarter of 2006. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2004, the Company had forward currency exchange contracts outstanding to exchange 11 million British Pounds for $21.1 million, which expired in the first quarter of 2005.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify> &nbsp;
</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><I>Interest Rate Risk</I></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Company&#146;s commercial paper outstanding of $247.5 million at December 31, 2005 is also subject to market risk as the debt reaches maturity and is reissued at prevailing interest rates. &nbsp;At December 31, 2005, interest rates outstanding ranged from 3.98% to 4.42%, with a weighted-average of 4.34%. &nbsp;At December 31, 2005 the Company had $224.9 million of fixed rate bonds outstanding, which mature in February 2008. &nbsp;A change in the market interest rate impacts the fair value of the instrument but has no impact on earnings or cash flows.</P>

<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:10pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:2.5pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>MANAGEMENT&#146;S RESPONSIBILITY FOR FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>To the Stockholders of Dow Jones &amp; Company, Inc.:</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Management has prepared and is responsible for the Company&#146;s consolidated financial statements and related information appearing in this report. &nbsp;The financial statements, which include amounts based on estimates and judgments that Management believes are reasonable, have been prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles consistently applied. &nbsp;Accordingly, Management believes that the consolidated financial statements reasonably present the Company&#146;s financial position and results of operations and that the form and substance of transactions are fairly reflected. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Management has developed and continues to maintain a system of internal accounting and other controls for the Company and its subsidiaries. &nbsp;Management believes these controls provide reasonable assurance that assets are safeguarded from loss or unauthorized use and that the Company's financial records are a reliable basis for preparing the financial statements. &nbsp;The Company's system of internal controls is supported by written policies, including a code of conduct, a program of internal audits, and by a program of selecting and training qualified staff. &nbsp;Underlying the concept of reasonable assurance is the premise that the cost of control should not exceed the benefit derived.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, an independent registered public accounting firm, audited the consolidated financial statements of the Company and its internal control over financial reporting, as described in their report. &nbsp;Their report expresses an opinion on whether the financial statements included in the Form 10-K present fairly, in all material respects, the financial condition of the Company and the results of its operations and its cash flows in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America and opinions on management&#146;s assessment of the effectiveness of the Company&#146;s internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2005 and on the effectiveness of the Company&#146;s internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2005 based on criteria established in <I>Internal Control - Integrated Framework</I> issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO).</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>The Board of Directors of the Company, through its audit committee consisting solely of independent directors, is responsible for reviewing and monitoring the Company's financial reporting, accounting practices and the retention of the independent registered public accounting firm. &nbsp;The audit committee meets regularly with financial management, internal auditors and the independent registered public accounting firm - - both separately and together - - to review the results of their audits, the adequacy of internal accounting controls and financial reporting matters.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>MANAGEMENT&#146;S ASSESSMENT OF INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL REPORTING</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Our management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting, as such term is defined in Exchange Act Rule 13a-15(f). Under the supervision and with the participation of our management, including our principal executive officer and principal financial officer, we conducted an evaluation of the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting based on the framework in <I>Internal Control &#150; Integrated Framework</I> issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. &nbsp;Based on our evaluation under the framework in <I>Internal Control &#150; Integrated Framework</I>, our management concluded that our internal control over financial reporting was effective as of December 31, 2005. &nbsp;PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, the independent registered public accounting firm that audited the financial statements included in this annual report on Form 10-K, has issued an attestation report on our management's assessment of internal control over financial reporting.</P>

<P style="page-break-before:always; margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><B>REPORT OF INDEPENDENT REGISTERED PUBLIC ACCOUNTING FIRM</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>To the Board of Directors and Stockholders of Dow Jones &amp; Company, Inc.:</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>We have completed integrated audits of Dow Jones &amp; Company, Inc.&#146;s 2005 and 2004 consolidated financial statements and of its internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2005 and an audit of its 2003 consolidated financial statements in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). &nbsp;Our opinions, based on our audits, are presented below.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><U>Consolidated financial statements and financial statement schedule</U></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements listed in the index appearing under Item 15(a)(1) present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of Dow Jones &amp; Company, Inc. and its subsidiaries at December 31, 2005 and 2004, and the results of their operations and their cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended December 31, 2005 in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. &nbsp;In addition, in our opinion, the financial statement schedule listed in the index appearing under Item 15(a)(2) presents fairly, in all material respects, the information set forth therein when read in conjunction with the related consolidated financial statements. &nbsp;These financial statements and financial statement schedule are the responsibility of the Company&#146;s management. &nbsp;Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements and financial statement schedule based on our audits. &nbsp;We conducted our audits of these statements in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). &nbsp;Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement. &nbsp;An audit of financial statements includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements, assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, and evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. &nbsp;We believe that our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><U>Internal control over financial reporting</U></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Also, in our opinion, management&#146;s assessment, included in Management&#146;s Assessment of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting appearing under Item 8, that the Company maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2005 based on criteria established in <I>Internal Control - Integrated Framework </I>issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO), is fairly stated, in all material respects, based on those criteria. &nbsp;Furthermore, in our opinion, the Company maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2005, based on criteria established in <I>Internal Control - Integrated Framework </I>issued by the COSO. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s management is responsible for maintaining effective internal control over financial reporting and for its assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting. &nbsp;Our responsibility is to express opinions on management&#146;s assessment and on the effectiveness of the Company&#146;s internal control over financial reporting based on our audit. We conducted our audit of internal control over financial reporting in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). &nbsp;Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether effective internal control over financial reporting was maintained in all material respects. &nbsp;An audit of internal control over financial reporting includes obtaining an understanding of internal control over financial reporting, evaluating management&#146;s assessment, testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control, and performing such other procedures as we consider necessary in the circumstances. &nbsp;We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinions. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>A company&#146;s internal control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. &nbsp;A company&#146;s internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that (i) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (ii) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorizations of management and directors of the company; and (iii) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the company&#146;s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify>Because of its inherent limitations, internal control over financial reporting may not prevent or detect misstatements. &nbsp;Also, projections of any evaluation of effectiveness to future periods are subject to the risk that controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0pt; margin-right:54pt; margin-bottom:0pt; width:558pt; font-family:Times New Roman" align=justify><BR></P>
